title: Prayer for a peaceful mind in refuting Manichaean heresy
english: I have prayed, and I still pray, to the one true almighty God, from whom are all things, through whom are all things, in whom are all things, that in refuting and disproving your heresy, Mani—to which you have perhaps attached yourselves more imprudently than maliciously—he would give me a mind made peaceful and tranquil, one that thinks more about your correction than about your overthrow. For although the Lord overthrows the kingdoms of error through his servants, he commands that the people themselves, insofar as they are people, are to be amended rather than destroyed. And whatever is divinely avenged before that final judgment—whether through the wicked or the righteous, whether through the ignorant or the knowing, whether secretly or openly—we must believe that it avails not for the destruction of human beings but for their medicine. Those who reject that medicine are being prepared for the final punishment.

Therefore, since in this whole universe of things some things have power for bodily punishment, such as fire, poison, disease, and others of this kind, and other things by which the soul is punished within itself not by troubles of its body but by the snares of its own desires, such as loss, exile, bereavement, insult, and things like these, while still other things are not torments but rather fomentations and soothing remedies for the sick, such as consolations, exhortations, disputations, and whatever else there may be—of all these, the highest justice of God works some even through the wicked who do not know what they do, and others through the good who do know. It was ours, then, to choose and desire the better things, so that we might have access to your correction, not in contention and rivalry and persecutions, but by consoling gently, exhorting kindly, disputing mildly. As it is written: "The Lord's servant must not quarrel, but be gentle to everyone, teachable, patient, correcting opponents with gentleness" (2 Timothy 2:24–25). It was ours, then, to want to seek this part; it is God's to grant what is good to those who will and ask.
orientation: Augustine opens the treatise by praying to the one true God and explaining that he seeks the correction, not the destruction, of the Manichaeans.

title: Only the ignorant rage against you
english: Let those rage against you who do not know with what labor truth is found and how difficult it is to avoid errors. Let those rage against you who do not know how rare and arduous it is to overcome carnal fantasies by the serenity of a pious mind. Let those rage against you who do not know with what difficulty the eye of the inner man is healed, so that it can look upon its own sun—not this one you worship in a heavenly body, shining and radiant to the fleshly eyes of both humans and beasts, but that one of which it was said through the prophet: “The sun of justice has risen for me” (Malachi 4:2), and of which it was said in the gospel: “He was the true light, which enlightens every man coming into this world” (John 1:9). Let those rage against you who do not know with what sighs and groans it comes about that God can be understood from however small a part. Finally, let those rage against you who have never been deceived by such an error as the one in which they see you deceived.
orientation: Augustine is addressing the Manichaeans, explaining that those who attack them harshly do so because they do not know how hard it is to find truth, avoid error, and be healed from false imaginings.

title: Augustine's patience toward Manichaeans and his demand for a fair inquiry
english: But I—after being tossed about for a long time and in many ways, I was at last able to look back and see what that purity is which is grasped without the telling of an empty story; I, who with difficulty and only by the Lord's help, wretched as I was, deserved to refute the empty imaginations of my own mind, gathered together from various opinions and errors; I, who so late submitted myself to the most merciful physician as he called and coaxed me, so that the fog of my mind might be wiped away; I, who wept for a long time so that the unchangeable and immaculate substance might deign to persuade itself to me inwardly, with the divine books joining their voice; I, finally, who both sought out all those fictions carefully that hold you entangled and bound by long habit, and listened to them attentively, and believed them rashly, and persuaded others of them as insistently as I could, and defended them against others stubbornly and passionately—I cannot rage against you at all. whom I must now bear with just as I then bore with myself, and deal with you with as much patience as my neighbors dealt with me, when I was wandering rabid and blind in your teaching.

But so that you may more easily become gentle, and not oppose me with a hostile spirit that is also destructive to yourselves, I must obtain this from you, with any judge you like: that all arrogance be set aside on both sides. Let none of us say that he has already found the truth; let us seek it as if it were unknown to both sides. For it can be sought diligently and harmoniously only if it is not believed by any rash presumption to have already been found and known. Or if I cannot obtain this from you, at least grant me this: that I now hear you for the first time as people unknown to me, and now examine you for the first time. I think what I ask is just, with this condition certainly kept: that I do not pray with you, do not hold assemblies with you, do not take the name of Manichaean—unless you give me a clear account, without any fog, of everything that pertains to the soul's salvation.
orientation: Augustine is speaking in his own voice, addressing the Manichaeans directly, explaining why he cannot rage against them and setting the terms for a joint search for truth.

title: What holds me in the Catholic Church
english: For in the Catholic Church—to say nothing of the most sincere wisdom, to the knowledge of which few spiritual people attain in this life, so that they know it at least in part, because they are human, but still without doubt; for the rest of the crowd, it is not liveliness of understanding but simplicity of believing that makes them most safe—to say nothing, then, of this wisdom, which you do not believe is in the Catholic Church, there are many other things that most justly hold me in her bosom. The agreement of peoples and nations holds me; the authority begun by miracles, nourished by hope, increased by love, and made firm by age holds me; the succession of priests from the very seat of the apostle Peter, to whom the Lord after his resurrection entrusted his sheep to be fed, down to the present episcopate holds me; and finally, the very name Catholic holds me, which not without reason this Church alone has obtained among so many heresies, so that although all heretics want to be called catholic, when some stranger asks where the Catholic Church gathers, no heretic dares to point to his own basilica or house. These, then, so many and so great, are the dearest bonds of the Christian name that rightly hold a person believing in the Catholic Church, even if, because of the slowness of our understanding or the merit of our life, the truth does not yet show itself most openly. But among you, where there is none of this to invite and hold me, only the promise of truth sounds aloud. If that truth is shown so clearly that it cannot come into doubt, it is to be preferred to all those things by which I am held in the Catholic Church. But if it is merely promised and not delivered, no one will move me from that faith which binds my soul to the Christian religion by so many and such great ties.
orientation: Augustine is addressing the Manichaeans, explaining why he remains in the Catholic Church before he examines Mani's Fundamental Letter.

title: Why Augustine will not believe Mani without proof
english: Let us see, then, what Mani teaches me, and let us look especially at that book you call the Letter of the Foundation, where almost everything you believe is contained. Indeed, when it was read to us in that wretched time, you told us we were illuminated. It certainly begins like this: “Mani, apostle of Jesus Christ by the providence of God the Father. These are wholesome words from the perennial and living fountain.” Now, with good patience, if you please, pay attention to what I am asking. I do not believe that this man is an apostle of Christ. Please do not be angry and start speaking harshly. You know that I have resolved to believe nothing rashly that you bring forward. So I ask: who is this Mani? You will answer: an apostle of Christ. I do not believe it; and now you will have nothing left to say or do. You were promising knowledge of the truth, and now you are forcing me to believe what I do not know. Perhaps you are about to read me the gospel and try to establish Mani’s identity from it. But if you found someone who did not yet believe the gospel, what would you do if he said to you, “I do not believe”? I myself would not believe the gospel unless the authority of the Catholic Church moved me.

So if I obeyed those who said to me, “Believe the gospel,” why should I not obey those who say to me, “Do not believe the Manichaeans”? Choose what you want. If you say, “Believe the Catholics,” they themselves warn me to give no faith to you; therefore, believing them, I cannot but not believe you. If you say, “Do not believe the Catholics,” you will not do rightly to force me through the gospel to Mani’s faith, because I believed the gospel itself when the Catholics preached it. But if you say, “You were right to believe the Catholics when they praised the gospel, but you were not right to believe them when they blamed Mani,” do you think me so foolish that, with no reason given, I should believe what you want and not believe what you reject? I act far more justly and cautiously if, since I once believed the Catholics, I do not come over to you unless you order me not to believe them, but make me know something most openly and clearly. Therefore, if you are going to give me a reason, set the gospel aside. If you hold to the gospel, I will hold to those at whose command I believed the gospel, and at their command I will not believe you at all. But if by chance you can find something in the gospel most clear about Mani’s apostleship, you will weaken for me the authority of the Catholics, who command me not to believe you; and once that authority is weakened, I will no longer be able to believe the gospel either, because it was through them that I believed it. So whatever you bring forward from it will have no weight with me. Therefore, if nothing clear about Mani’s apostleship is found in the gospel, I will believe the Catholics rather than you. But if you read something clear from it in Mani’s favor, I will believe neither them nor you: not them, because they lied to me about you; and not you, because you are offering me the very Scripture I believed through them, and they lied to me. But far be it from me not to believe the gospel. For believing it, I do not find how I can also believe you; the names of the apostles that are read there do not include the name of Mani among them. And who succeeded in the place of Christ’s betrayer we read in the Acts of the Apostles; and I must believe that book if I believe the gospel, since the Catholic authority commends both Scriptures to me alike. In that same book we also have the well-known history of Paul’s calling and apostleship. Read to me now, if you can, where in the gospel Mani is called an apostle, or in any other book that I confess I have already believed. Or will you read the passage where the Lord promised the apostles the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete? Look at that passage and see how many and how great are the things that call me back and deter me from believing Mani.
orientation: Augustine has just recalled how he was called 'illuminated' when Mani's Fundamental Letter was read to him, and now he begins to test Mani's claim to be an apostle of Jesus Christ.

title: Why Mani calls himself apostle of Jesus Christ rather than of the Paraclete
english: For I ask why the beginning of this letter is: Mani, apostle of Jesus Christ, and not: the Paraclete, apostle of Jesus Christ. If the Paraclete was sent by Christ and then sent Mani, why do I read: Mani, apostle of Jesus Christ, and not rather: Mani, apostle of the Paraclete? If you say that he is Christ himself, who is also the Holy Spirit, you contradict the Scripture itself, where the Lord says: and I will send you another Paraclete (John 14:16). But if you think the name of Christ is rightly placed, not because he is Christ who is also the Paraclete, but because both are of the same substance—that is, not because he is one, but because they are one—then Paul could also have said: Paul, apostle of God the Father, because the Lord said: I and the Father are one (John 10:30). Nowhere does he say this, nor does any of the apostles write that he is an apostle of the Father. What then does this novelty mean? Does it not seem to you to smell of some deceit or other? Certainly if he judged that it made no difference, why does he not vary his title in other letters, calling himself apostle of Christ in some and apostle of the Paraclete in others? But I have always heard apostle of Christ, whenever I have heard it, and apostle of the Paraclete not even once. What do we suppose is the reason for this, except that that pride, the mother of all heretics, drove the man to want to appear not as one sent by the Paraclete, but as one so taken up that he himself would be called the Paraclete? Just as Jesus Christ, a man, was not sent by the Son of God—that is, by the power and wisdom of God, through which all things were made—but was so taken up according to the Catholic faith that he himself was the Son of God, that is, that in him the very wisdom of God appeared for the healing of sinners: so that man wanted to appear to have been taken up by the Holy Spirit, whom Christ promised, so that now when we hear Mani called the Holy Spirit, we understand him to be an apostle of Jesus Christ, that is, one sent by Jesus Christ, who promised that he would send him. Singular audacity this and unspeakable sacrilege!
orientation: Augustine is questioning the opening title of Mani's Fundamental Letter, where Mani names himself 'apostle of Jesus Christ' rather than 'apostle of the Paraclete.'

title: Why Mani's birth from two sexes should not shame the Spirit if the virgin birth shames Wisdom
english: But still I ask: since Father and Son and Holy Spirit are joined with a nature not unlike, as even we confess, why do you not think it shameful to preach that the man Mani, taken up by the Holy Spirit, was born from both sexes, while you fear to believe that the man taken up by the only-begotten Wisdom of God was born of a virgin? If human flesh, if the intercourse of a man, if the womb of a woman could not defile the Holy Spirit, how could the womb of a virgin defile the Wisdom of God? So this Mani, who boasts in the Holy Spirit and in the gospel reading, must necessarily grant you either that he was sent by the Holy Spirit or that he was taken up. If he was sent, let him call himself an apostle of the Paraclete; if he was taken up, let him grant a human mother to him whom the only-begotten Son of God took up, if he also grants a father to him whom the Holy Spirit took up. Let him believe that the Word of God was not polluted by Mary's virginity, if he urges us to believe that the Holy Spirit could not be polluted by his parents' intercourse. But if you say that Mani was taken up by the Holy Spirit not in the womb or before the womb but after he was already born, it is enough that you admit he had flesh produced from a man and a woman. For since you do not fear Mani's flesh and blood coming from human intercourse, and his intestines full of dung, which that flesh carried, and you do not believe the Holy Spirit was contaminated by all these things—the Spirit by whom you believe that man was taken up—why should I dread a virginal womb and untouched genital parts, and not rather believe that the Wisdom of God remained unstained and pure within those maternal organs when the man was assumed? Therefore, since whether your Mani claims he was sent or taken up by the Paraclete, he will be able to establish neither, I am now more cautious and believe he was neither sent nor taken up.
orientation: Augustine is addressing the Manichaeans directly, pressing the inconsistency between their claim that the Holy Spirit took up Mani, who was born from a man and a woman, and their refusal to believe that God's Wisdom took up a man born of a virgin.

title: Mani's self-presentation and the Bema festival
english: For when he added the words “by the providence of God the Father,” what else was he aiming at, after naming Jesus Christ—whose apostle he calls himself—and God the Father, by whose providence he says he was sent by the Son, than to make us believe that he himself is the third person, the Holy Spirit? This is how he writes: “Mani, apostle of Jesus Christ by the providence of God the Father.” The Holy Spirit is not named, though he above all ought to have been named by the man who commends his apostleship to us by the promise of the Paraclete, so that he may press down the inexperienced with the authority of the gospel. When you are asked about this, you answer that when Mani is named as apostle, the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, is named, because he deigned to come in him. So I ask, as I was saying above, why you shudder when the Catholic Church says that the one in whom divine Wisdom came was born of a virgin, while you feel no shudder at all that the one in whom you proclaim the Holy Spirit came was born from a woman joined with a man. What else I should suspect, I do not know, except that this Mani, who seeks access to the minds of the inexperienced through the name of Christ, wanted himself to be worshipped in place of Christ himself. I will say briefly how I infer this. When I often asked you, in the time when I was listening to you, what the reason was that you generally observed the Lord’s Passover with no celebration at all, or sometimes with a very lukewarm one from a few people—with no vigils, no longer fast enjoined on the hearers, no more festive display—while you honor your Bema festival, that is, the day on which Mani was killed, with great honors, with a tribunal furnished with five steps and adorned with costly linens, set out in full view and presented to those who worship: when I asked this, the answer was that the day of the passion of the one who truly suffered should be celebrated; but Christ, who was not born and showed not true but feigned flesh to human eyes, did not undergo but feigned his passion. Who would not groan at men who want to be called Christians, who fear that truth may be polluted from a virgin’s womb, and do not fear pollution from a lie? But to return to the matter: who would not suspect, if he paid careful attention, that Mani denied that Christ was born of a woman and had a human body for this reason—so that his passion, which is now the most festive season of the whole world, would not be celebrated by those who had believed Mani, and so that the longed-for solemnity of his own death day would be honored with such great devotion? For this was what pleased us most in that Bema festival celebration: it was observed in place of the Passover, because we desired that feast day more intensely when the other, which used to be sweetest, had been taken away.
orientation: Augustine is addressing the Manichaeans, arguing that Mani's opening self-description as 'apostle of Jesus Christ by the providence of God the Father' is a ploy to make himself worshipped in place of Christ.

title: The Holy Spirit's coming is proven from Acts
english: Perhaps you will say to me: when, then, did the promised Paraclete come from the Lord? If I had nothing else to believe, I would more readily wait for him still to come than admit that he came through Mani. But as it is, since the coming of the Holy Spirit is proclaimed with complete clarity in the Acts of the Apostles, what necessity forces me to believe heretics so dangerously and so easily? For in that book it is written as follows: “In the first book, Theophilus, I dealt with all that Jesus began to do and teach until the day when he chose the apostles through the Holy Spirit and commanded them to preach the gospel. After his passion he presented himself alive to them by many proofs over a period of days, appearing to them during forty days and teaching about the kingdom of God. He stayed with them and commanded them not to depart from Jerusalem, but to wait for the promise of the Father, ‘which,’ he said, ‘you heard from my mouth; for John baptized with water, but you will begin to be baptized with the Holy Spirit, whom you are also to receive not many days from now, until Pentecost.’ So when they had come together, they asked him, ‘Lord, will you be restored at this time, and when will the kingdom of Israel be?’ But he said, ‘No one can know the time that the Father has set by his own authority; but you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria and to the end of the earth’” (Acts 1:1-8). Here you have the place where he reminded the disciples of the Father’s promise, which they had heard from his mouth about the coming of the Holy Spirit. Now let us see when he was sent. A little later the text continues and says: “When the day of Pentecost was fulfilled, they were all together in one place with one accord; and suddenly there came from heaven a sound as of a violent wind rushing, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting; and divided tongues as of fire appeared to them and settled upon each one of them. And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance. Now there were dwelling in Jerusalem Jews, devout men from every nation under heaven. And when this sound occurred, the crowd gathered and was bewildered, because each one heard them speaking in his own language. And they were amazed and astonished, saying to one another, ‘Are not all these who are speaking Galileans? And how is it that we hear, each of us, the language in which we were born? Parthians, Medes, Elamites, and residents of Mesopotamia, Armenia, Cappadocia, Pontus, Asia, Phrygia, Pamphylia, Egypt, and the regions of Africa near Cyrene; and Romans who had come, and Jewish inhabitants, Cretans and Arabs—we hear them telling in our own languages the mighty works of God.’ And they were amazed and perplexed at what had happened, saying, ‘What does this mean?’ But others mocked and said, ‘They are all loaded with new wine’” (Acts 2:1-13). See where the Holy Spirit came. What more do you want? If the Scriptures are to be believed, why should I not rather believe these, which are confirmed by the most robust authority, which along with the gospel itself—where we equally believe the Holy Spirit was promised—deserved to become known to the peoples, to be commended to posterity, and to be preached? When I read these Acts of the Apostles, joined to the gospel with equal authority, I find not only that the Holy Spirit was promised to those true apostles, but also that he was sent so manifestly that no room was left for error on this matter.
orientation: Augustine is answering a Manichaean objection that the Paraclete promised by the Lord has not yet come, by appealing to the Acts of the Apostles.

title: The Spirit Given After Christ's Glorification
english: The glorification of our Lord among human beings is his resurrection from the dead and his ascension into heaven. In the gospel itself it is written, according to John: “The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John 7:39). If the Spirit had not yet been given for this reason, because Jesus had not yet been glorified, then once Jesus was glorified the Spirit was necessarily given at once. And because of that twofold glorification, according to man and according to God, the Holy Spirit was also given twice: once after he rose from the dead, when he breathed into the face of the disciples and said, “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22); and again after he ascended into heaven, ten days having passed. That number signifies perfection, since the Trinity of the Creator is added to the sevenfold number by which all created things hold together. Spiritual men discuss many things about these matters with reverence and care. But I will not depart from my purpose. I undertook to deal with you in such a way that I would not teach you—which you perhaps consider arrogant—but that I would seem to be eager to learn from you what I could not learn in nine years. So I have writings I can believe about the coming of the Holy Spirit. If you forbid me to believe them, so that I do not rashly believe what I do not know—for that is how you usually warn—then I will believe your writings far less. So either take all books out of the way and by arguing lay open the truth, about which I cannot doubt, or produce books of such a kind that what I am to believe is not imposed on me with arrogance, but what I am to learn is shown to me without deceit. Perhaps, you say, this letter is such a book. I do not want to linger any longer on its threshold. Let us look at what is inside.
orientation: Augustine is still arguing from the Acts of the Apostles that the Holy Spirit was demonstrably sent to the true apostles, and now turns to the Gospel of John to show the Spirit was given after Jesus was glorified.

title: Mani's opening promises and blessings are common to truth and deceit
english: “These,” Mani says, “are health-bringing words from a perennial and living fountain. Whoever hears them and first believes them, and then keeps what they instill, will never be liable to death, but will enjoy eternal and glorious life. For surely the one who has been instructed in this divine knowledge, through which he is set free and will remain in everlasting life, must be judged blessed.” And this, as you see, is a promise, not yet an exhibition of the truth. You too can very easily notice that under this veil any errors at all can be colored over, so that they creep secretly into the minds of the inexperienced through an adorned doorway. If he had said, “These are pestilential words from a poisonous fountain; whoever hears them and first believes them, and then keeps what they instill, will never be restored to life, but will be struck with a penal and wretched death—for surely the one who has been entangled in this infernal ignorance, through which he is plunged down and will remain in everlasting torments, must be judged miserable”—if he had said this, he would have spoken the truth, but he would not only have won no reader for this book; he would have stirred everyone whose hands it fell into to the greatest hatred. Therefore let us pass on to what follows, and let these things not deceive us, since they can be words common to good and bad, learned and unlearned alike. What follows then?

“May the peace,” he says, “of the invisible God and the knowledge of the truth be with the holy and most dear brothers who alike believe and serve the heavenly commands.” May it be as he says, for this too is a kind and most acceptable wish. Only let us remember that these things can be said by good teachers and by deceivers alike. So if he said nothing but such things, I would grant that he should be read and embraced by all. Nor would I disapprove of what follows next, for he adds: “But may the right hand of light also guard you and rescue you from every evil assault and from the snares of the world.” And in general, whatever is written at the beginning of this letter, until it comes to the matter at hand, I do not wish to criticize, lest much effort be spent on minor points. Let us now look at the man’s most evident promise.
orientation: Augustine has just entered the text of Mani's Fundamental Letter and now quotes its opening promises and blessing, then shows that such words could be spoken by either good teachers or deceivers.

title: Mani's promise of certain knowledge about Adam and Eve
english: So then, he says, dearest brother Patticus, about what you indicated to me when you said you wanted to know what sort of birth Adam and Eve had—whether they were produced by word alone, or begotten from a body—I will answer you as is fitting. For this matter has been inserted and recorded in various scriptures and revelations by many people in dissimilar ways. Therefore the truth of this matter, as it has itself, is unknown by almost all nations, and by all who have even disputed long and much about it. For if clear knowledge of the generation of Adam and Eve had come about for them, they would never have been subject to corruption and death.

So he promises us clear knowledge of this matter, so that we will not be subjected to corruption and death. And if that is still not enough, see what follows. “Therefore,” he says, “many things must be mentioned beforehand so that one may arrive at this mystery without any ambiguity.” This is what I was saying: the truth must be shown to me in such a way that I may arrive at it without any ambiguity. Even if he himself did not promise it, I ought still to demand and insist on it, so that for so great a reward of evident and most certain knowledge I would not be ashamed to become a Manichaean from a Catholic Christian, no matter who contradicted me. So now let us hear what he brings forward.

“So if it seems good to you,” he says, “listen first to what existed before the constitution of the world and how the battle was waged, so that you may be able to separate the nature of light and of darkness.” Now he has proposed things that are unbelievable and entirely false. For who would believe that any battle was fought before the constitution of the world? And yet, even if it were believable, we should want not to believe, but to know. For someone who says that the Persians and Scythians fought a war with each other many years ago says something believable, but we can only believe it as something heard or read, not know it as experienced and grasped. Since I would reject him if he said something of that sort—for he did not promise things I would be forced to believe, but things I could know without any ambiguity—how shall I not reject him when he says things that are not only uncertain but even unbelievable? But what then? What if he makes them clear and known by some reasoning? Let us hear, then, if we can, with all patience and gentleness, what follows.
orientation: Augustine has just finished quoting the opening wishes of Mani's Fundamental Letter and now turns to Mani's central promise of certain knowledge, quoting Mani's reply to Patticus about the birth of Adam and Eve.

title: Mani's description of the two substances and the land of light
english:
"For these," Mani says, "were in the beginning two substances divided from each other. And God the Father held the kingdom of light, perpetual in his holy stock, magnificent in power, true in his very nature, always rejoicing in his own eternity, containing with himself wisdom and vital senses, through which he also comprehends the twelve members of his light—namely, the flowing riches of his own kingdom. And in each one of his members are hidden thousands of innumerable and immeasurable treasures. The Father himself, however, preeminent in his own praise, incomprehensible in greatness, has joined to himself blessed and glorious ages that can be estimated neither by number nor by length, with whom this same holy and illustrious Father and begetter dwells, with no one in his distinguished kingdoms either lacking or placed in a lowly position. And so his most splendid kingdoms are founded upon the bright and blessed land, that they can never be moved or shaken by anyone."

How is he going to prove these things to me, or how did he himself come to know them? Do not frighten me with the name of the Paraclete. First, because I came to you not to believe unknown things but to know certain things, having been made more timid by you yourselves.
orientation: Augustine has just quoted the opening of Mani's Fundamental Letter, where Mani describes the two eternal substances, and now Augustine challenges Mani to prove these claims.

title: Faith and knowledge: Mani cannot prove either his Spirit-claim or his message
english: You yourselves know how fiercely you are in the habit of insulting those who believe rashly, especially since the very man who has now begun to narrate uncertain things promised a full and firm knowledge a little earlier.

Then again, if faith is to be commanded to me, I am more frightened by that Scripture where I read that the Holy Spirit came and inspired the apostles, to whom the Lord had promised he would send him (Acts 2:1-4; John 14:26). Therefore either prove to me that the things he says are true, so that you may show what I cannot believe, or prove to me that the one who speaks is the Holy Spirit, so that I may believe what you cannot show.

For my part, I profess the Catholic faith, and through it I presume that I will arrive at certain knowledge. But you, who try to weaken my faith, hand over certain knowledge if you can, so that you may convict me of having believed rashly what I believed. There are two things you offer me: one, when you say that the one who speaks is the Holy Spirit, and the other, when you say that the things he speaks are manifest. I ought to know both from you without any doubt; but I am not greedy—teach me one of them. Show that this man is the Holy Spirit, and I will believe that what he says is true, even if I do not know it; or show that what he says is true, and I will believe that he is the Holy Spirit, even if I do not know it. Could anyone deal with you more fairly or more kindly? But you can show neither the one nor the other. You have chosen nothing else but to praise what you believe and ridicule what I believe.

Since I in turn will have praised what I believe and ridiculed what you believe, what do you think we should judge or do, except to abandon those who invite us to know certain things and afterward command us to believe uncertain things, and to follow those who invite us first to believe what we are not yet able to see, so that, made stronger by that very faith, we may merit to understand what we believe—no longer through men, but through God himself illuminating and strengthening our mind within?

And since I have asked how he proves it to me, I now ask how he himself came to know it. If he says that it was revealed to him by the Holy Spirit and that his mind was divinely illuminated so that he might know the things he says as certain and manifest, he himself indicates what the difference is between knowing and believing. For he himself knows, since these things are shown to him most openly; but to those to whom he narrates them, he does not instill knowledge, but persuades belief. Whoever rashly agrees with him becomes a Manichaean, not by knowing certain things, but by believing uncertain things—just as he once deceived us when we were inexperienced young men.

Therefore he ought not to have promised us knowledge, nor manifest cognition, nor arrival at the matter in question without any ambiguity, but rather to say that these things were shown to him, and that those to whom they are narrated ought to believe him about things they do not know. But if he said that, who would not answer him: If I am going to believe unknown things, why should I not rather believe those things that are already celebrated by the agreement of learned and unlearned alike and are established among all peoples by the weightiest authority? Fearing that this would be said to him, he pours clouds over the inexperienced, first promising knowledge of certain things, and afterward commanding faith in uncertain things. Yet if this is said to him—that he should at least teach that these things were shown even to himself—he likewise fails, and orders us to believe this too. Who could bear such deceit and such arrogance?
orientation: Augustine is addressing Mani directly, challenging the claim that Mani is the Paraclete and that his teachings are certain knowledge rather than objects of faith.

title: Mani's five pestilential natures and the folly of a bodily God
english: What if, with God and our Lord helping me, I show that what he says is not only uncertain but false? What could be found more wretched than this superstition, which not only fails to provide the knowledge and truth it promises, but says things that are violently opposed to knowledge and truth? This will appear more clearly in what follows. For he says: “Along one side and border of that illustrious and holy land was the land of darkness, deep and immense in size, in which dwelt fiery bodies—pestilential races, that is. Here were infinite darknesses flowing from the same nature, immeasurable, with their own offspring; beyond these were muddy and turbid waters with their inhabitants; within these were horrible and violent winds with their prince and parents. Again, a fiery and corruptible region with its leaders and nations. In the same manner, further inward, a race full of darkness and smoke, in which dwelt the monstrous prince of all and leader, having around him innumerable princes, of all of whom he himself was the mind and origin. These were the five natures of the pestilential land.”

If he said that the nature of God is an airy or even ethereal body, he would certainly be laughed at by all who are able to perceive, with some sharpness of an already more serene mind, that the nature of wisdom and truth is not stretched out or spread through any spaces of place, is great and magnificent without any bulk, is not smaller in one part and larger in another, but is equal to the highest Father in all things, and does not have one thing here and another elsewhere, but is whole everywhere and present everywhere.
orientation: Augustine has just shown that Mani demands belief in unproved claims; now he quotes Mani's description of the land of darkness and its five natures, then argues that any bodily account of God's nature is absurd.

title: The soul is not extended through space
english: But what shall I say of truth and wisdom, which surpass every power of the soul, when the nature of the soul itself, which is found to be mutable, in no way occupies the spaces of places with some bulk of its own? For whatever has any thickness cannot help but be diminished through its parts, having one thing here and another elsewhere. A finger is smaller than the whole hand, and one finger is smaller than two, and this finger is in one place, that finger in another, and the rest of the hand elsewhere. We see this not only in the jointed masses of bodies, but also in the earth: this part of it is not where that part is, because each part occupies its own place. A smaller part of moisture occupies a smaller place, a larger part a larger place; one part is near the bottom, another near the rim of the cup. Likewise the parts of air each fill their own places. Nor can it happen that the air which fills this house can at the same time have within the same house also that air which the neighbors have. Of light itself, one part pours in through this window, another through that one, and more through a larger window, less through a smaller one. Nor can there be any body at all—whether heavenly or earthly, airy or moist—that is not less in its part than in its whole, nor can it in any way have another part at the same time in the place of this part. Rather, having one thing here and another elsewhere, it is stretched out through whatever spaces of places with a distant and divided, or rather, so to speak, cuttable bulk.

But the nature of the soul—even if we consider not that power of it by which it understands truth, but that lower power by which it holds the body together and senses in the body—is in no way found to be stretched out through the spaces of places by any bulk. For it is wholly present to each single particle of its body, since it senses wholly in each one. Its part in the finger is not smaller and its part in the arm larger, as the finger itself is smaller than the arm; rather, it is as great everywhere because it is wholly everywhere. For when the finger is touched, it does not sense through the whole body, and yet it senses wholly. That touch does not escape the whole of it, which would not happen unless it were wholly present. Nor is it wholly present in such a way that, when the finger is touched and it senses in the finger, it abandons the rest of the body and gathers itself to that one place where it senses. But when it senses wholly in the finger of the hand, if another place is touched on the foot, it does not cease to sense wholly there either. And so in single distant places it is wholly present at the same time—not abandoning one place so that it may be wholly in another, nor holding both in such a way that it has one part here and another elsewhere, but able to present itself wholly to single places at the same time. Since it senses wholly in each one, it shows clearly enough that it is not held by the spaces of places.
orientation: Augustine is arguing against Mani's picture of God as a bodily mass, and now turns to the soul to show that even a mutable nature is not spread out through places.

title: Memory of bodily things and the mind's power over images
english: What if we think of memory not of intelligible things but of these bodily things? Even beasts are perceived to have this kind of memory. Beasts of burden travel without error through places they know, and wild animals return to their dens. Dogs recognize the bodies of their masters, and when asleep they often murmur and sometimes burst into barking. They could not do any of this unless images of things seen or somehow sensed through the body were moving about in their memory. Who can worthily conceive where these images are received, where they are carried, or where they are formed? If they could not be larger than the size of our body allows, someone might say that the soul forms and preserves these images within the very spaces of its own body, in which she too is enclosed. But as it is, though the body occupies a very small part of the earth, the mind ranges through images of immense regions of heaven and earth. As these images depart and succeed one another in crowds, the mind is not made narrow by them. Here it shows itself not to be spread out through places, because it is not, so to speak, contained by images of the largest places, but rather contains them—not by some fold, but by ineffable power by which it can add anything to them and take anything away, contract them into a narrow space, expand them through immensity, arrange them as it wills, throw them into disorder, multiply them, and reduce them to fewness or singleness.
orientation: Augustine is arguing that the mind is not spread out through space, and here he considers memory of bodily things, which even animals have, to show that the mind contains images of vast places without being extended through them.

title: The mind's judging power surpasses all spatial images
english: Why should I speak now of that power by which truth is understood—the power that resists with great vigor those very images drawn from the senses of the body and shaped in the mind, when they set themselves up in place of the truth? By this power one sees that the real Carthage is one thing, and another is the Carthage the mind imagines and changes with total ease as it pleases. From that same ease come the countless worlds through which the thought of Epicurus wandered without number. And, not to pursue many examples, from that same ease comes that land of light spread through infinite spaces, and the five caves of the nation of darkness with their inhabitants, in which the Manichaeans' fantasies have dared to claim for themselves the name of truth. What then is this power that discerns these things? However great it may be, it is greater than all of them, and it is thought without any such imagining of things. Find spaces for it, if you can. Spread it through places. Distend it with the swelling of an infinite mass. If you think rightly, you cannot. For whatever of that kind occurs to you, you judge by that very thought that it can be cut into parts, and you make one part smaller there, another larger, as much as you please. But that very thing by which you judge these things, you see is above them—not by height of place, but by dignity of power.
orientation: Augustine is arguing that the mind is not spread out through space, and now turns to the power by which it judges truth and resists false images, including Mani's land of light.

title: The soul's power over space shows what God must be
english: So if you perceive that the soul, so often changeable—whether through a crowd of shifting wills, or through feelings that bend it this way and that according to the abundance or lack of things, or through the countless games of fantasies, or through forgetfulness and memory, or through learning and inexperience—if, as I said, you perceive that the soul, so often changeable through these and similar motions, is not spread out and extended through places, but surpasses all such spaces by the liveliness of its power, then what must be thought or judged about God himself? He remains unshaken and unchangeable above all rational minds, giving to each what is due to each. The soul dares to speak of him more easily than to see him, and the more purely it is able to see him, the less it speaks of him. Yet if, as the Manichaeans' fantasies make a din, he were stretched out through places—bounded on one side, but of infinite extent on the others—then however many particles and countless bits in him, some larger, some smaller, could be measured at the whim of the one thinking, so that, for example, a two-foot part in him would be eight parts smaller than a ten-foot part. For this must happen to all natures that are spread through such spaces and cannot be wholly everywhere. But this is not found in the soul itself, and it is believed about it in a deformed and shameful way only by those who are unable to consider these things.
orientation: Augustine is arguing against the Manichaean picture of God as a body spread through space, using the soul's non-spatial power of judgment as a clue to God's nature.

title: Mani's 'one side' implies other sides
english: But perhaps one should not deal with carnal minds in this way. Instead, one must descend to the thoughts of those who either do not dare or are not yet able to pursue an incorporeal and spiritual nature by thinking, so that they do not even consider their own thought by that same thought and find that it judges about spatial distances without itself occupying any space. So let us descend to their level of sense and ask them: next to which part, or next to which side, as Mani says, was the land of darkness located in relation to that illustrious and holy land? For he says, "next to one part and side," but he does not say which part or which side—right or left. But whichever they choose, one thing is certainly clear: you cannot speak of one side unless there is another side. And where there are three or more sides, either you mean a boundary of a shape that is enclosed on every side, or, if it opens out into immensity on some side, it must still be bounded on the sides that are called sides. So let them say what was joined to the land of light on the other side or sides, if the nation of darkness was on one side. They do not say. But when they are pressed to say, they say that the other sides of that land they call the land of light are infinite—that is, that it stretches out through infinite spaces and is held in by no limit. And they do not understand that then there are no longer sides, which is perfectly obvious even to the slowest minds. For there would be sides only if they were bounded by their own limits. "What does it matter to me," he says, "if there are no sides?" But when you said "next to one part and side," you forced us to understand another part or parts and another side or sides. For if there was only one side, you should have said only "next to the side," not "next to one side." Just as in our body we correctly say that something is next to one eye, because there is another eye, or next to one breast, because there is another. But if we say next to one nose or next to one navel, when there is no other, both the learned and the unlearned will laugh at us. But I am not pressing you on words; perhaps you wanted to call one as if unique.
orientation: Augustine is addressing Mani's claim that the land of darkness lay beside one side of the land of light, and he is now descending to the level of carnal-minded readers to show that the phrase 'one side' is self-contradictory.

title: Two lands joined at their sides must both be bodies
english: What, then, was next to the side of that land you call bright and holy? The land of darkness, Mani says. What? Do you at least admit that this land was corporeal? You have to say this, since you claim that all bodies take their origin from it. So I ask you: however slow, however carnal you are, have you never even noticed that these two lands could not be joined to each other at their sides unless both were corporeal? Why, then, were we told—through some perverse blindness, I do not know—that only the land of darkness was or is corporeal, while the one called the land of light must be believed to be incorporeal and spiritual? Let us wake up at last, good people, and, now that we have been reminded, at least notice what is very easy to see: two lands cannot be joined at their sides unless each is a body.

But if we are still too dense and slow even for this, I ask whether the land of darkness itself had one side and was infinite in all other directions, like the land of light. They do not believe that, for they are afraid it might seem equal to God. So they say it is immense in depth and in length, but above it they assert there are spaces of infinite emptiness. And so that it may not seem to occupy even a single share while the land of light occupies a double one, they narrow it on two sides as well. It is as if a single loaf—for what is being said can be seen more easily this way—were formed crosswise into four quarters, of which three are white and one is black. Now take away the division between the three white quarters and make them infinite upward and downward and everywhere backward: that is how they believe the land of light to be. Then make the one black quarter infinite downward and backward, but with immense emptiness above it: that is how they imagine the land of darkness. But they show these things as if they were secrets to the excessively attentive and those who inquire diligently.
orientation: Augustine is quoting and then attacking Mani's description of the land of light and the land of darkness as two lands joined at one side.

title: The land of light is penetrated by the land of darkness
english: But if that is so, it appears that the land of darkness is touched by the land of light on two sides; and certainly if it is touched on two sides, it also touches on two sides. At any rate, the land of darkness lay along one side.

Then how ugly the shape of the land of light appears: like a split hoof with a black wedge pressed in beneath it, bounded only on the side where it is split, while above it gapes open with emptiness between, immense as it is from the surface of the land of darkness upward. How much better, then, the shape of the land of darkness itself is shown to be, since the one splits and the other is split; the one is inserted and the other lies open between; the one gives no place within itself to any emptiness, while the other is compact only on its lower side, where the hostile wedge fills it from beneath. Therefore unlearned and greedy men, since they give greater honor to the multitude of parts than to unity—so as to give six parts to the land of light, three downward and three upward—preferred that the land of light be penetrated rather than penetrate. For with such a shape, even if they deny it was mixed, they cannot deny it was penetrated.
orientation: Augustine continues his spatial critique of Mani's two eternal lands, now showing that the land of darkness touches and penetrates the land of light on two sides.

title: Comparing Catholic and Manichaean ways of imagining God
english: Now compare not the spiritual men of the Catholic faith—in whom, as far as the mind can in this life, it discerns that the divine substance and nature is stretched out through no spaces of place and shaped by no dimensions of outline—but compare our carnal and little ones, who, when they hear certain members of our body spoken of in allegory—as when the eyes of God and the ears of God are mentioned—are accustomed to picture God to themselves by the freedom of fantasy in the form of a human body. Compare these with those Manichaeans who are accustomed to describe these trifles to attentive and curious men as if they were great secrets, and consider. Which of them think more tolerably and honorably about God: those who think of him in human form, endowed with the highest dignity in its kind, or those who think of him spread out in an infinite mass—yet not on every side, but infinite and dense on three sides, and on one side split, open, gaping, loose above with emptiness, wedged below by the land of darkness—or, if it is better to say it this way, open above by his own nature, entered below by an alien nature? See, I join you in mocking carnal men who cannot yet think spiritual things and suppose God to be in human form. Mock with me, if you can, those who imagine so deformed and foul a split or tear in God, so emptily gaping above, so dishonorably plugged below, in most wretched thought. For this difference also exists: those carnal ones who think of God in human form, if they remain content in the bosom of the Catholic Church and are to be nourished with milk, do not hurl themselves into rash opinions, but nourish there a devout zeal for seeking, there ask that they may receive, there knock that it may be opened to them (Matthew 7:7), and they begin to understand spiritually the allegories and parables of the Scriptures and gradually to perceive that the divine powers are fittingly expressed sometimes by the name of ears, sometimes of eyes, sometimes of hands or feet or even of wings and feathers, and also of shield and sword and helmet and countless other such things. The more they advance in this understanding, the more firmly Catholic they become. But the Manichaeans, when they have abandoned the imagination of that shape, will not be able to be Manichaeans. For they attribute this as the peculiar and preeminent praise of their founder: they say that those divine mysteries which were placed figuratively in the books of the ancients were reserved for this one who was to come last, to be unlocked and demonstrated, and that for this reason no teacher would come from God after him, because he said nothing through figures and allegories, since he both opened the things of the ancients that were of that kind and displayed his own things clearly and without knots. Therefore these men have no interpretations to which they can return when it is read to them from their own founder: 'Along one part and side of that illustrious and holy land was the land of darkness.' Wherever they turn, constrained by the misery of their fantasies, they must fall into splits or abrupt cuttings and joinings or most shameful props—things which it is most wretched to believe, I will not say of the unchangeable nature of God, but of any incorporeal nature, however changeable, such as the soul. And yet, if I could not raise myself to higher things nor unfold my thoughts from the false imaginations which I carry fixed in memory through the bodily senses into the freedom and purity of spiritual nature, how much better would I think of God in the form of a human body than fasten that black wedge to the lower split of him and, finding nothing with which to plug the vast upper looseness, leave it gaping and open with immense emptiness? What is more foul than this opinion? What more dark than this error can be said or imagined?
orientation: Augustine is addressing the Manichaeans directly, contrasting how unspiritual Catholics and Manichaeans each picture God, and arguing that even the crude Catholic imagination is more honorable than the Manichaean image of a split and penetrated divine mass.

title: Mani's threefold land of light collapses into one nature, which the wedge of darkness penetrates
english: Next, since I read of God the Father, and of his kingdoms founded upon the bright and blessed land, I want someone to tell me whether the Father, his kingdoms, and the land are of one and the same substance and nature. If that is so, then that wedge of the race of darkness no longer splits and penetrates what is, as it were, another nature that is the body of God—which itself would be foul with unspeakable deformity—but that wedge of the land of darkness splits and penetrates the very nature of God itself. Think about this, I beg you—you are human beings—think about this and flee; and with torn hearts, if it can be done, root these sacrileges of such fantasies out of your faith and drive them away. Or will you say that those three are not of one and the same nature, but that the Father has one nature, the kingdoms another, and the land another, so that each has its own distinct natures and substances, ordered by degrees of excellence? If that is true, Mani should have proclaimed not two natures but four. But if the Father and the kingdoms have one nature, and the land alone has a different one, then three natures should have been proclaimed. Or if he preferred to say two because the land of darkness does not belong to God, I ask how the land of light does belong to God. For if it has a different nature and he neither begot it nor made it, it does not belong to him, and his kingdoms are located in another's property. Or if it belongs to him because it is nearby, then the land of darkness also belongs to him, since it not only touches the land of light by nearness but even furrows it by penetration. But if he begot it, then we ought not to believe that it has a different nature. For what God has begotten, we ought to believe is what God is, as the Catholic Church believes concerning the only-begotten Son. And so necessity drives you back to that foulness to be fled and detested: that the black wedge splits not the land as something other and different, but the very nature of God. But if God did not beget the land but made it, I ask from what he made it. If from himself, what else is that but begetting? If from some other nature, I ask whether it was good or evil. If good, then there was some good nature that did not belong to God—which you will never dare to say. If evil, then that race of darkness was not the only evil nature. Or perhaps God had already taken some part from it, which he turned into the land of light and upon which he established his kingdoms? Then he should have done this with the whole of it, so that no evil nature would remain. But if he did not make the land of light from another substance, it remains that he made it from nothing.
orientation: Augustine is addressing the Manichaeans directly, pressing the implications of Mani's own words about God the Father and his kingdoms founded upon the bright and blessed land.

title: Mani's land of light must be made from nothing
english: So if you are now persuaded that almighty God can make something good from nothing, come into the Catholic Church and learn that all the natures God made and established are arranged in ranks of excellence from the highest to the lowest, all of them good, but some better than others. They were made from nothing when God the craftsman worked through his wisdom with power, so to speak, so that what did not exist could come to exist, and insofar as it existed it was good; but insofar as it fell short, it showed that it was not begotten from God but made by him from nothing. If you think it through, you will find nothing that holds you back. For you cannot say that the land of light you describe is what God is, lest the foulness of that wedge be forced into God's own nature. You cannot say it was begotten from him, lest it likewise be understood to be what God is and fall back into the same deformity. You cannot say it is foreign to him, lest you be compelled to say he set up his kingdom in something foreign to him and to speak of not two but three natures. And you cannot say he made it from a foreign substance, lest there be some other good besides God or some evil besides the race of darkness. What remains, then, is for you to confess that God made the land of light from nothing—and you refuse to believe it. But if God could make from nothing some great good that was nevertheless lower than himself, then because he is good and begrudges no good thing, he could also make a second good lower than the first. He could make a third, ranked below the second, and so on down to the lowest good in the order of created natures, until the whole of them stood firm, fixed by a definite limit rather than flowing apart in an indefinite number, uncertain. Or if you refuse to confess that God made even that land of light from nothing, you will have no way out, no escape from such great foulness and such sacrilegious opinions.

Or at least consider this, since fleshly thought is free to imagine whatever fantasies it pleases: perhaps you can find some other shape for this joining of the two lands, so that such a detestable and abhorrent picture does not come to mind—the land of God, whether of the same nature as God or of a different one, in which God's kingdom is founded, lying stretched out in an immense mass through infinite space, so that it lies with its limbs extended and spread open through infinity, by which limbs, most foully and shamefully from below, it receives even that inserted wedge of the land of darkness, itself of immense size. But whatever other shape you find for how these two lands are joined together, you certainly cannot erase the letter of Mani. I do not mean the other letters in which he described these things more explicitly—perhaps because fewer people know them, they seem to carry less danger. I mean this very letter of the Foundation that we are now discussing, which is generally best known to nearly all those among you who are called enlightened. For here it is written: "Along one side and flank of that illustrious and holy land was the land of darkness, deep and of immense size."
orientation: Augustine is addressing the Manichaeans directly, pressing them on the origin of the land of light described in Mani's Fundamental Letter.

title: The geometry of the two lands refutes Mani's myth
english: What more are we waiting for? We have it in our grasp: we hold what was alongside the side. Now invent whatever shapes you like and sketch whatever outlines you please, but that immense mass of the land of darkness was certainly joined to the land of light either by a straight side, or a curved one, or a twisted one. But if it was twisted, then the holy land also has a twisted side. For if the holy land has a straight side and is touched by the twisted side of the other, deep caverns lie open between them, empty through infinite space, and the emptiness was no longer only above the land of darkness, as we used to hear. And if that is so, how much better it would have been for the land of light to withdraw a little farther away and let so great an emptiness lie between, so that it could not be touched by the land of darkness on any side at all! Indeed, so great a space of empty depth would lie open that if any shamelessness arose from that nation—even if the princes of darkness recklessly wished to leap across to it, since bodies cannot fly unless they are supported by bodily air—they would be hurled headlong through that emptiness, and because it would be infinite in the downward direction, they would never reach any bottom. Even if they could live forever, they could never do harm while they were always being carried downward. But if it was joined by a curved side, then the land of light received it in a curved hollow, and that was a deformed embrace. Or if the other land was curved inward like the shape of a theater, it clasped the curved part of the land of light in such a hollow with a coupling no less deformed. Or if the one had a curved side and the other a straight one, it did not touch it along the whole side. And certainly it would have been better, as I said above, for it not to touch on any side, and for so much emptiness to lie between that it would separate the two lands by a proper interval and allow the reckless and shameless, hurled headlong through the infinite, to do no harm. But if a straight side touched a straight side, I do not see any receptacles or gaps, but I plainly see such great peace and such great concord between the two lands that no greater joining could exist. For what is more beautiful, what more fitting, than for straight to be coupled to straight in such a way that no hollow or bend anywhere breaks or divides a natural and stable joining through infinite space and from infinite eternity? The straight sides of both lands, even if they were separated by an intervening emptiness, would not only be beautiful in themselves because they were so straight, but with the interval placed between they would correspond to each other in such a way that the equal straightnesses on this side and that, even without any joining, would come together into one beauty by their very likeness. But when this joining is added, what could be more harmonious and peaceful than these two lands, and what more beautiful than the very coupling of two straight sides could be said or thought? I cannot find it.
orientation: Augustine is examining Mani's Fundamental Letter, where Mani says the land of darkness lay along one side and flank of the land of light, and now Augustine presses the spatial implications of that claim.

title: Rectitude as a good in the land of darkness
english: What am I to do with souls so miserably entangled in perverse error and habit? These people do not know what they are saying when they say these things; they do not pay attention. I ask you, no one is forcing you, no one is pressing you into a contest, no one is mocking your past errors—except the one who has not experienced God's mercy. To be rid of errors, let us work only toward this: that they may at some point come to an end. Look at this for a little while without hostility and bitterness—we are all human; let us hate not ourselves but errors and falsehoods—please, look at it for a little while. God of mercies, help those who look, and kindle an inner light for those who seek the truth. For what do we understand, if we do not understand that straight is better than crooked?

So I ask you, if you will receive this calmly and modestly: if someone were to make crooked the straight side of the land of darkness, which is joined to the straight side of the land of light, would he not take away some of its beauty? You must admit—unless you want to bark—that not only is its beauty taken away if it is made crooked, but also the beauty it could have shared with the straight side of the land of light. So if someone takes that away and makes the straight crooked, so that what was in harmony now clashes and what fit together now recoils, would he remove any substance from it? Learn from this, then, that evil is not a substance. In a body, when its form changes for the worse, its form is lost or rather diminished, and what was previously called beautiful is called ugly, and a body that previously pleased now displeases. So in the soul, the honor of a right will—by which one lives piously and justly—is made crooked when the will changes for the worse. By that sin the soul becomes miserable, though it held blessedness through the honor of a right will, with no substance added or taken away.

Next, consider this too: even if we grant that for other reasons the side of the land of darkness is evil—because it is dark, because it is shadowy, or whatever else can be said—it is not evil in the fact that it is straight. Just as I grant that there is something evil in its color, so you must grant that there is something good in its straightness. It is therefore sacrilege to alienate this good, however great it is, from God the artificer, from whom comes every good in any nature; unless we believe this, we go astray most ruinously. How then does Mani say that this land is the supreme evil, when in the straightness of its side I find a good of no small beauty, as far as body is concerned, and he wants it to be utterly alien from the almighty and best God? To whom else should we attribute that very good which we find in it, if not to the author of all goods? Can we find anyone else?

But that side was evil too, he says. Suppose it was evil: it would certainly be worse if it were not straight but distorted. How then is it the supreme evil, if something worse than it can be thought? Furthermore, there must be some good whose loss makes any thing worse. By losing straightness that side would become worse; therefore straightness, some good, is in it. And you will never tell me where it comes from unless you take refuge in him from whom we confess that all goods come, whether great or small. But let us now pass from the consideration of this side to other matters.
orientation: Augustine is addressing the Manichaeans directly, asking them to consider whether the straight side of the land of darkness contains a good that cannot be attributed to the supreme evil.

title: The five natures and their inhabitants in the land of darkness
english: In that fiery land, he says, dwelt bodies—that is, pestilential kinds. When he says “dwelt,” he certainly wants us to understand them as animate and living. But so that I do not seem to quibble over a word, let us look at how he distributes all those inhabitants of that land into five living kinds. Here, he says, were infinite darknesses, flowing from the same nature, immeasurable, with their own offspring; beyond them were muddy and turbulent waters with their own inhabitants; within these were horrible and violent winds with their prince and parents. Again, a fiery and corruptible region with its own leaders and nations. In the same manner, further inward, a race full of gloom and smoke, in which dwelt the immense prince of all and leader, having around him innumerable princes, of all of whom he himself was the mind and origin. And these were the five natures of the pestilential land.

We notice five natures as parts of one nature, which he calls the pestilential land. These are darkness, waters, winds, fire, and smoke. He arranges these five natures so that darkness is outermost, from which he begins to count. Within the darkness he places the waters; within the waters, the winds; within the winds, fire; within the fire, smoke. And these five natures each had their own kinds of inhabitants, which are likewise five. For I ask whether there was one kind of inhabitant in all five natures, or different kinds, just as the natures themselves are different. They answer that they were different, and they teach from other books that the darkness had serpents; the waters had swimming creatures, such as fish; the winds had flying creatures, such as birds; the fire had quadrupeds, such as horses, lions, and others of this sort; the smoke had bipeds, such as human beings.
orientation: Augustine is quoting and analyzing Mani's description of the land of darkness, which Mani divides into five natures—darkness, waters, winds, fire, and smoke—each with its own kind of inhabitants.

title: The ordered goods of the land of darkness
english: Who, then, arranged these things? Who distributed and distinguished them? Who gave them number, quality, forms, and life? For all these things are good through themselves, and no source is found from which they may be assigned to any nature except from God, the author of all goods. It is not as when poets are accustomed to describe chaos, or in whatever way they suggest a certain formless matter, without quality, without measures, without number and weight, without order and distinction—some confused thing utterly devoid of all quality, which certain Greek teachers call apoion. No, these people do not try to suggest their so-called land of darkness in that way at all, but in an entirely different, far divergent, and contrary manner: they join side to side and align them. They count five natures, distinguish them, arrange them, declare them by their own proper qualities, and do not leave them deserted and barren, but fill them with their own inhabitants, and to those inhabitants they attribute forms suited to them and adapted to their dwellings—and what surpasses all these, life. To enumerate such great goods and yet say they are alien to God, the author of all goods—this is to fail to recognize in things so great a good of order, and in oneself so great an evil of error.
orientation: Augustine is examining Mani's description of the land of darkness and arguing that the goods Mani attributes to it cannot come from anywhere but God.

title: Mani's five evil natures are full of goods
english: But these five kinds, he says, that inhabit those natures were savage and pestilential. As if I had praised savagery and pestilence in them. Look, I join you in blaming what you charge as evil in them; you join me in praising what you yourself record as good in them. Then you will see that you want to establish goods mixed with evils as the supreme and extreme evil. I join you in blaming the pestilence there; join me in praising the health there. For those kinds could not have been born, or nourished, or inhabited that land without some health. I join you in blaming the darkness there; join me in praising the fruitfulness there. For you call the darkness immeasurable, and yet you add that it has its own offspring—although darkness is not bodily, and this whole name is the absence of light, just as nakedness is the lack of clothing and emptiness is the lack of bodily fullness. For that reason darkness could produce nothing, although a dark land—that is, a land lacking light—could produce something. But let us set that aside for now. Yet where offspring come forth, there is a temperament suited to health, and a numerous concord orders and builds together into unity the limbs of those being born, each agreeing with the others in a peace of moderation. Who does not understand that all these things deserve greater praise than the darkness deserves blame? I join you in blaming the turbid filth of the waters there; join me in praising the very form and quality of the waters, and the agreeing limbs of the swimming inhabitants, the life holding and ruling the body, and every temperament of its kind suited to well-being. However much you reproach the muddy and turbid waters, by the very fact that you call them such waters that they could produce and contain their own living creatures, you cannot take away from them the form of some kind of body and the likeness of parts by which they are formed and brought into peace into one quality—because if you take that away, there will be no body at all. All these things, if you are human, you perceive are praiseworthy. And however much you exaggerate the savagery of those inhabitants and their attacks of tearing and devastation upon one another, you still do not take away from them the numerous defining limits of their forms, by which each of their bodies is brought to peace through the equality of its limbs, nor the temperament of health, nor the governing of the soul drawing the parts of its body into a unity of friendship and concord. If you look at these things with human perception, you see they are more praiseworthy than the things that displease are blameworthy. I join you in blaming the horror of the winds there; join me in praising the breathable and nourishing nature of those same winds, and the form of a body with the fitting agreement of continuous and extended parts. By all these things they could produce and nourish their inhabitants and keep them in health—and among those inhabitants, along with the other things praised in all living creatures by the reasoning above, there is especially their tireless and easy passage from where they wish to where they wish, and the concordant thrust of their wings in flight and their not-unequal motion. I join you in blaming the corruption of the fire there; join me in praising the fire that generates and thrives, and its timely temperament for those being born, so that they could grow together, and be perfected in their own numbers and lineaments, and live and dwell there. All these things you recognize are to be admired and praised not only in the dwelling place of the fire, but also in the inhabitants themselves. I join you in blaming the obscurity of the smoke and the monstrousness of the prince who, as you say, lingered in it; join me in praising that even in the smoke itself you find no part unlike the others, by which in its own kind it preserves the agreement and measure of its parts among themselves, so that what it is, it is by a certain unity. No one considers this soberly without praising it with wonder. And what of this? You even add to the smoke the force and power of generating, when you assign to it its own princely inhabitants, so that what we have never seen here, there the smoke is fruitful and offers a healthy dwelling to its inhabitants.
orientation: Augustine is answering Mani's description of the five natures inhabiting the land of darkness as savage and pestilential, arguing that the very things Mani lists contain goods that cannot belong to a supreme evil.

title: The prince of smoke also shows ordered good
english: Even in that prince of smoke himself you noticed only one thing. You saw his monstrousness, so you could condemn him. Should you not have looked at all the rest? It would have forced you to praise his nature. He had a soul and a body. The soul gave life, and the body breathed with that life. The soul ruled, and the body obeyed. The soul led, and the body followed. The soul held him together, and the body did not fall apart. The soul moved in rhythm, and the body stood firm in the joined frame of its many limbs. Does the ordered peace or the peaceful order in this one prince not move you to praise?

What I have said of this one prince holds for all the rest. He was savage and monstrous toward others. I do not praise that. I praise all those great goods you refuse to notice. Anyone who believed Mani without thinking should look at those goods now, even if he needs prompting. If he looks and weighs them, he will know without doubt what he is speaking of.
