When he speaks of these natures, he speaks of certain good things. They are not the highest and unmade goods, as God is, one Trinity. They are not made goods set high in the order, as the holy angels and the most blessed powers are. They are the lowest goods, set at the bottom of things in the measure proper to their kind.

The unskilled condemn them only because they compare them with higher things. They see how much good these lower things lack, a good the higher things possess. They give the name of evil to the absence of that same good. I speak of these natures in this way for one reason. Mani names things we already know in this world. We know darkness and waters and winds and fire and smoke. We also know crawling animals and swimming and flying animals, and four-footed and two-footed animals. Take darkness out of that list. Darkness is nothing but the absence of light, as I have said. The eye tells it apart by not seeing, as the ear tells silence apart by not hearing. That is not because darkness is something, but because light is absent, just as it is not because silence is something, but because sound is absent. Apart from darkness, all the rest in that list are natures, and everyone knows them. Their form is praiseworthy and good in whatever measure it exists. No wise person separates that form from God, the author of all good things.
orientation: Augustine is speaking, pressing his argument that every nature insofar as it exists is good by examining Mani's prince of smoke.

title: Mani's beasts in the darkness refuted
english: Mani stands exposed as wholly false in his wish to arrange the natures he learned here in his fantasies, as if into a race of darkness. First, darkness can beget nothing, as I have said.

He answers, "Those darknesses were not like the darkness you know here." From where, then, do you teach me about them? Or do you, so wordy a promiser of teaching, perhaps force me to believe? Suppose I believe him. I still know this much. If those darknesses had no form, just as the darkness here has none, they could generate nothing. If they had form, they were better. Yet when he says they were not like these, he wants us to believe in something worse. He might as well say that silence, which is to the ears what darkness is to the eyes, begot deaf or mute animals there. Then, when told that silence is no nature, he would answer, "But not the kind of silence you know here." In that way you would say whatever you pleased to those you had once tricked into believing you.

Although what led him to invent crawling creatures born in darkness could indeed have been well noticed in the very first stirrings of newborn creatures. But some serpents see sharply and exult so much in the presence of light that they seem to testify heavily against him. It was easy to discern swimming creatures here in the waters and transfer fantasies to them, and so too with flying creatures in the winds, since we call the push of this thicker air, where birds fly, wind. Why it entered his mind to invent four-footed animals in fire, I do not know. He did not say it without a reason, but he paid too little heed and went badly wrong. His followers usually give this reason. Four-footed animals are voracious and burn strongly for mating. But many men outdo any four-footed animal in voracity, and men are certainly two-footed, and Mani calls them sons not of fire but of smoke.

Nothing is readily found more voracious than geese. He may place them in smoke because they have two feet, or in the waters because they love to swim, or in the winds because they have feathers and sometimes fly. By his own division they certainly do not belong to fire. On burning for mating, I think he watched neighing horses drag toward mares with bitten bridles. He rushed to write down what he saw and ignored the house sparrow. Beside that sparrow any stallion looks icy cold.

When asked why Mani put two-footed creatures in smoke, they answer that the race of two-footed creatures is lofty and proud. Men draw their origin from there, they say. Smoke rises into the air in a ball and seems swollen, so they judged it not absurdly like the proud. That observation could have served to supply a likeness of proud men, to frame an allegory or grasp one. It should not make us believe that two-footed living creatures were born in smoke and from smoke. By the same logic they should have been born in dust, for dust often rises to the sky with no less swirl and lift. They should have been born in mists, for mists often breathe up from the earth so that watchers far off cannot tell smoke from mist.

Finally, why draw the argument in waters and winds from the fact that dwelling can be endured to the dwellers? We see swimming creatures live in the waters and flying creatures live in the winds. Did fire and smoke not check this liar with shame? He set such dwellers there that nothing more absurd could be set. Fire burns a four-footed animal and corrupts it, and smoke chokes two-footed creatures and kills them. By this fact alone he must admit that he makes those natures better in the race of darkness, where he wants us to believe all is worse. There fire begot the four-footed animal and fed it and kept it safely, even comfortably. Likewise smoke bore its own two-footed children from a most gentle fold and raised them without trouble, with life-giving care, all the way to that princedom, and kept them there. So these lies stand exposed by the things we see in the world. They were conceived by a careless and unskilled fleshly sense, labored out by fantasies, and rashly uttered and written down, and they have swelled the number of heretics.
orientation: Augustine is speaking, refuting Mani's arrangement of crawling, swimming, flying, four-footed and two-footed creatures in the land of darkness.

title: Goods and evils in the land of darkness
english: But they must be pressed more by that line of argument, so that they may understand, if they can, how truly it is said in the Catholic Church that God is the author of all natures. I was dealing with this line of argument above, when I said: I join you in blaming the plague, the blindness, the turbid filthiness, the horrible violence, the corruptibility, the savagery of the rulers, and things like these. But you join me in praising form, distinction, ordering, peace, the unity of forms, the congruence of members and their equalities in number, the vital breathings and nourishments, the tempering of health, the rule and guidance of the soul and the service of bodies, the likeness and harmony of parts in each nature—both those that inhabited and those that were inhabited—and other things of this kind. For in this way they understand, if they are willing to pay attention without stubbornness, that they themselves are already mixing goods and evils when they speak about that land where they believed there was only supreme evil, and so that if the things that were listed as evils are taken away, the goods that were praised remain without any blame, but that if the goods themselves are taken away, no nature remains. From this, whoever can see now sees that every nature, insofar as it is a nature, is good. For from one and the same thing, in which I found what to praise and he found what to blame, if the things that are good are taken away, there will be no nature; but if the things that displease are taken away, an incorrupt nature will remain. Take from waters that they be filthy and turbid, and pure and tranquil waters remain. Take from waters the harmony of their parts, and they will not be waters. If, therefore, when that evil is removed a purer nature remains, but when the good is taken away no nature remains, then what makes a nature there is the good it has; and what is evil is not a nature, but against nature. Take from winds the dread and excessive force that displeases you, and you can think of winds that are gentle and moderate. Take from winds the likeness of their parts, by which their body is joined into unity and made at peace with itself so that it is a body, and no nature will remain for you to think of. It would take long to go through the rest. But it is clear to those who judge without any partisan zeal that when these natures are mentioned, certain things are attached to them that cause displeasure; and when we remove those things, better natures remain. From this it is understood that they are good insofar as they are natures, because when you take away from them in turn everything good that they have, no natures will exist. Notice also, you who wish to judge rightly, that savage ruler himself. If his savagery is taken away, consider how many praiseworthy things remain: the frame of his body, the congruence of his members on this side and that, the unity and peace of his form with its parts woven together, the order and arrangement of the soul that rules and gives life and of the body that serves and is given life. If all these things are taken away—and any others I may have failed to list—no nature at all will remain.
orientation: Augustine is arguing that the Manichaean land of darkness cannot be pure evil, because it contains goods that remain when its evils are removed.

title: Goods inseparable from natures, and the error of hating a whole nature
english: But perhaps you will say that those evils cannot be removed from such natures, and therefore they must be accepted as natural. The question now is not what can or cannot be removed, but certainly it is no small light for understanding that all natures, insofar as they are natures, are good—because those goods can be thought of without those evils, yet no nature can be thought of without those goods. For I can think of waters without the disturbance of mud, but without the peace of parts joined together no form of a body occurs to the mind or can be perceived in any way. And therefore not even those muddy waters could exist without this good—the good by which it was brought about that some bodily nature could exist. For when you say that those evils cannot be removed from such natures, the answer is that those goods also cannot be removed from such natures. Why then do you want to call these things natural evils because of the evils you think cannot be removed, yet you do not want to call them natural goods because of the goods you are proven unable to remove?

It remains for you to ask—for this is usually your final word—where those evils come from, which I too said displeased me. Perhaps I will answer, if you first tell me where those goods come from, which you too are compelled to praise, unless you wish to be of the most absurd heart. But why should I ask this, when both of us confess that all goods, whatever and however great they are, come from the one God, who is supremely good? Resist then, you yourselves, against Mani, who judged that so many and such great goods—which we have recalled and rightly praised: the peace and harmony of parts in each nature, the health and strength of living things, and the rest, which it now wearies me to repeat—exist in the fictitious land of darkness in such a way that he tried to alienate them from that God whom he confesses to be the author of all goods. For he did not see those goods, while he paid attention only to what displeased him. It is as if someone terrified by the roar of a lion, watching it drag and tear apart the bodies of animals or men it had seized, were struck by a certain childish weakness of mind with such great fear that he saw only the lion's savagery and ferocity, completely neglecting and passing over everything else about it, and cried out that the nature of that animal was not merely evil but a great evil—all the more exaggeratedly, the more timidly he spoke. But if he saw the lion led tame and gentle with its ferocity subdued—especially if he had never before been terrified by that beast—then he would have leisure to consider and praise the lion's beauty with security and without fear. About this I will say nothing except what most pertains to the matter: it can happen that some nature offends in one respect and hatred is born against the whole of it, when it is obvious that the form of a true and living beast is far better—even when it terrifies in the woods—than an imitated and counterfeit one, when it is praised painted on a wall. Therefore let him not deceive us by this error, nor make us blind to considering the forms of natures, when he finds fault with certain things in them in such a way that he forces us to dislike on every side what he cannot find fault with on every side. And composing our minds in this way to a fair judgment, let us now ask where the evils come from that exist alongside those goods—evils which I too said I disapproved of. We will see this more easily if we can bring them all together under one name.
orientation: Augustine is answering the imagined Manichaean objection that the evils in certain natures cannot be removed, and is about to ask where evil comes from.

title: Evil is corruption, not a nature
english: Who would doubt that the whole of what is called evil is nothing other than corruption? Different evils can be named with different words, but the evil of all things in which any evil can be noticed is corruption. The corruption of a skilled soul is called unskillfulness; the corruption of a prudent soul, imprudence; of a just soul, injustice; of a brave soul, cowardice; of a quiet and tranquil soul, desire or fear or sadness or boasting. Then in a living body, the corruption of health is pain and disease; the corruption of strength is weariness; the corruption of rest is labor. Then in the body itself alone, the corruption of beauty is ugliness; the corruption of straightness is crookedness; the corruption of order is perversity; the corruption of wholeness is splitting or breaking or diminution. It would be long and difficult to name every corruption of the things I have mentioned and of countless others, since many that are said to be in the body can also be said to be in the soul, and there are countless cases where corruption holds its own proper names. But it is now easy to see that corruption harms nothing except by weakening the natural state, and therefore it is not a nature but against nature. And if nothing is found in things as evil except corruption, and corruption is not a nature, then no nature is evil.

But if perhaps you cannot understand this, attend to this point: everything that is corrupted is diminished in some good, because if it were not corrupted, it would be uncorrupted; and if it could not be corrupted at all, it would be incorruptible. It is necessary, however, that if corruption is an evil, then either being uncorrupted or being incorruptible is a good. But now there is no question about an incorruptible nature; we are dealing with things that can be corrupted, which while they are not corrupted can be called uncorrupted, but cannot be called incorruptible. For only that is properly called incorruptible which not only is not corrupted but also cannot be corrupted in any part. Therefore whatever things are uncorrupted and yet can be corrupted, when they begin to be corrupted, are diminished in that very good by which they were uncorrupted—and indeed in a great good, because corruption is a great evil. And as long as corruption can increase in them, so long do they have a good by which they may be diminished. Therefore those natures which he pretends existed in the land of darkness either could be corrupted or could not. If they could not, they were incorruptible, than which good nothing is higher. If they could, they were either being corrupted or not being corrupted. If they were not being corrupted, they were uncorrupted, which we see cannot be said without great praise. But if they were being corrupted, they were diminished in that so great a good; if they were diminished in a good, they had a good by which they might be diminished. And if they had a good, those natures were not the supreme evil, and the whole story of Mani is false.
orientation: Augustine is now defining evil as corruption and applying this definition to Mani's land of darkness.

title: Where corruption comes from
english: But since we have asked what evil is, and have come to know that it is not a nature but contrary to nature, we must next ask where it comes from. If he had done this, he would perhaps have fallen less easily into such great error. For he hastily and in the wrong order asked where it comes from, not having first asked what it is. And so nothing could meet his searching except empty fantasies, from which a mind much fed by carnal senses is stripped only with difficulty. Someone who desires no longer to contend but not to err will say: where does this corruption come from, which we have found to be a kind of general evil of good things, but of good things that can be corrupted? Whoever asks this finds the answer quickly, if he seeks the truth with great ardor and knocks with constant, reverent perseverance. For through human beings some reminder can be made by signs and words; but the one true teacher, the incorruptible truth itself, the only interior teacher, teaches. He also became exterior, to call us back from exterior things to interior things, and receiving the form of a servant (Philippians 2:7), he deigned to appear humble to those lying low, that his sublimity might be known to those who rise. Let us be suppliants in his name, and let us seek these things by imploring the Father's mercy through him. First, a very brief answer can be given to those who ask where corruption comes from: it comes from this, that the natures which can be corrupted were not begotten from God, but were made by him from nothing. Since the reasoning above has shown that they are good, no one can rightly say, "God would not have made good things." But if someone says, 'He made them supremely good,' he must understand that the supreme good is he himself, who made these good things.
orientation: Augustine has just shown that evil is not a nature but against nature; now he asks where corruption comes from and answers that corruptible natures were made by God from nothing, not begotten from God.

title: Why God made other goods below himself
english: What harm would it do, you ask, if the things God made from nothing were also supremely good? And yet if one of us were asked, after accepting and believing in God the Father as the supreme good, whether there could be another supreme good and where it might piously be thought to come from, we could give no right answer except that it comes from God the Father, who is supremely good. So we must remember that what is from him was born from him, not made by him from nothing, and therefore it too is supremely good—that is, incorruptibly good. And we see that it is unjust to demand that the things he made from nothing should be as supremely good as the one he begot from himself, who is supremely good. If he had not begotten one alone, he would not have begotten what he himself is, because he himself is one. Therefore it is unskillful and impious to look for brothers for the only-begotten Son, through whom the Father made all good things from nothing, unless they are sought because he deigned to appear in human nature. For this reason he is called both only-begotten and first-born in the Scriptures: only-begotten from the Father, first-born from the dead. And, he says, we have seen his glory, the glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth (John 1:14). And Paul says: so that he might be the first-born among many brothers (Romans 8:29).

But if we were to say, "These good things that were made from nothing would no longer exist, but only God's nature would exist," we would be envying such great goods. It is an impious voice to think it an injury that a thing is not what God is, and therefore to wish that no good should exist because God is set above it. I ask you, nature of the rational soul, bear with being somewhat less than God is—and so much less that after him nothing is better than you. Bear with it, I say, and become gentle toward him, lest he drive you still further down into the depths, where through the narrow straits of punishment the good that you are may become utterly worthless to you. You are proud against God if you are indignant that he goes before you, and you think of him too insultingly if you do not rejoice beyond words that you are so great a good that he alone is more excellent than you.

Once this is settled and made firm, do not say: "God should have made my nature alone; I would not want any good to be made after me." For what is good after God need not already be the last. And here it becomes most evident how much dignity he gave you: God, who alone naturally rules over you, made other good things over which you too would rule. Do not be surprised that they do not now serve you in every way and sometimes even torment you, because your Lord has greater power over the things that serve you than you yourself do, as over the servants of his own servants. What wonder, then, if when you sinned—that is, when you did not obey your Lord—the things you ruled over became instruments of punishment for you? What is so just, and what is more just than God? For human nature deserved this in Adam, though this is not the place to discuss it. But still the just ruler is shown by just rewards and just punishments: by the blessedness of those who live rightly and the punishment of those who sin.

Yet you have not been abandoned without mercy, for you are called back to return by fixed measures of things and times. So by the right governance of the most high Creator one has come down even to earthly goods, which are corrupted and reformed, so that you might have comforts mixed with punishment, so that you might praise God when delighted by the order of good things, and flee back to him when trained by the experience of evils. In this way, insofar as earthly things serve you, they teach you that you are their mistress; but insofar as they trouble you, they teach you to serve your Lord.
orientation: Augustine is answering an imagined Manichaean objection that God should have made only himself, by explaining the order of goods and the rational soul's place below God.

title: Corruption is ordered by God for punishment and return
english: Therefore, although corruption is an evil and although it does not come from the creator of natures but from the fact that they were made from nothing, nevertheless even corruption itself, under the rule and governance of the one who made all things, is so ordered that it harms only the lowest natures, for the punishment of the damned and for the training and warning of those who are returning, so that they may cling to the incorruptible God and remain incorrupt. For this alone is our good, as it is said through the prophet: “But for me it is good to cling to God” (Psalm 72:28 (LXX/Vulgate numbering)). And do not say, “God would not make corruptible natures.” Insofar as they are natures, God made them; but insofar as they are corruptible, God did not make them. For corruption is not from him who alone is incorruptible. If you grasp this, give thanks to God; if you do not grasp it, be still and do not rashly condemn what you have not yet understood, but humbly attend to him who is the light of the mind, so that you may understand. For when we say “corruptible nature,” not one but two names are spoken. Likewise when we say “God made from nothing,” we hear not one but two names. So give back to each of these its own: when you hear “nature,” let it belong to God; when you hear “corruptible,” let it belong to nothing—yet in such a way that the corruptions themselves, although they are not from God’s art, are still in his power, to be arranged according to the order of things and the merits of souls. Therefore we rightly say that reward and punishment come from him. For his not making corruption still leaves him able to hand over to corruption the one who deserved to be corrupted—that is, to the one who first began to corrupt himself by sinning, so that he who willingly committed it when it enticed should feel torturing corruption against his will.
orientation: Augustine is concluding his argument that corruption is not from God as a nature but is ordered by God's governance for punishment and for calling souls back to him.

title: God as punisher, not corrupter
english: For it is not only in the Old Testament that it is written, “I make good things and create evils” (Isaiah 45:7), but even more clearly in the New, where the Lord says: “Do not fear those who kill the body and after that have nothing more they can do; but fear him who, after he has killed the body, has power to send the soul into hell” (Luke 12:4-5). And the apostle Paul bears the clearest witness that penal corruption is added to voluntary corruption by divine judgment, when he says: “For the temple of God is holy, and that temple you are; whoever corrupts the temple of God, God will corrupt him” (1 Corinthians 3:17). If this had been said in the old law, what attacks they would make, accusing God as a corrupter! Fearing that word, many Latin translators refused to say “God will corrupt him,” but said “God will destroy him,” and without departing from the reality they avoided the offense of the word. Yet these people would inveigh no less against God as a destroyer if they found this in the old law or the prophets. But they are refuted by the Greek copies, in which it is written most plainly: “Whoever corrupts the temple of God, God will corrupt him.” And if someone asks them how this is said, so that God is not thought a corrupter, they immediately explain that “he will corrupt” means “he will hand over to corruption,” or whatever other way they can. If they had this attitude toward the old law, they would understand many things there that are worthy of wonder, and things not yet understood they would not tear apart with hatred, but would defer them with honor.
orientation: Augustine is arguing that God justly adds penal corruption to voluntary corruption, and he defends the wording of 1 Corinthians 3:17 against Manichaean objections.

title: Corruption tends toward non-being; form tends toward being
english: But if someone does not yet believe that corruption is from nothing, let him set before himself these two things, “to be” and “not to be,” as if from opposite sides, for the sake of understanding—so that we may walk more slowly with the slow. Then let him place something in the middle, for example the body of a living creature, and ask himself this: while that body is being formed and born, while its form is increased, nourished, strengthened, made firm, adorned, and established—insofar as it endures and is made stable—toward which side does it tend, toward being or toward not being? He will not doubt that even in its very beginnings it is something, but the more it is established and made firm in form and beauty and strength, the more it comes to be, and it tends toward that side where being is placed. Now let it begin to be corrupted. Let all that stability be weakened, let its powers grow faint, let its strength waste away, let its form be disfigured, let the joining of its limbs fall apart, let the harmony of its parts waste away and dissolve. Let him ask now through this corruption where it tends, toward being or toward not being. I do not think him so blind and slow that he doubts what answer he should give himself, or fails to perceive that the more a thing is corrupted, the more it tends toward destruction. And everything that tends toward destruction tends toward not being. Since, then, we must believe that God unchangeably and incorruptibly is, and since it is clear that what is called nothing is utterly not being—and since you have set before yourself these two, being and not being, and have recognized that the more form is increased, the more a thing tends to be, and the more corruption is increased, the more it tends not to be—why do you hesitate to say, in any corruptible nature, what in it is from God and what is from nothing? For form is according to nature, and corruption is against nature. Because increased form compels being, and we confess that God supremely is; but increased corruption compels not being, and it is established that what is not is nothing. Why, I ask, do you hesitate to say, in a corruptible nature—which you call both a nature and corruptible—what is from God and what is from nothing? And why do you seek a nature contrary to God? If you confess that he supremely is, do you not see that not being is contrary to him?
orientation: Augustine is arguing that corruption comes from nothing, not from God, and asks the reader to test this by considering how a body tends toward being as its form grows and toward non-being as it is corrupted.

title: Why corruption removes what God gave
english: Why then, you say, does corruption take away what God gave to nature? It does not take it away except where God permits it; and he permits it where he judges it most orderly and most just, according to the degrees of things and the merits of souls. For the form of a spoken sound also passes away and is destroyed by silence; yet our speech is carried through by the departure and succession of passing words, and is fittingly and pleasantly distinguished by measured intervals of silence. So too the lowest beauty of temporal natures is carried through by the passing of things and distinguished by the death of what is born. If our sense and memory could grasp the order and measures of this beauty, it would please us so much that we would not dare to call the deficiencies by which it is distinguished corruptions. But in the part of that beauty where we labor, while the flowing temporal things we love desert us, we pay the penalties of sins and are reminded to love eternal things.
orientation: Augustine is answering an imagined Manichaean objection that corruption destroys what God gave to natures.

title: Seek the good above temporal beauty
english: So let us not seek in this beauty what it has not received. It is the lowest beauty precisely because it has not received what we seek, and for what it has received let us praise God, because he gave so great a good of form even to this beauty, low as it is. Yet he did not give it so that we should cling to it as its lovers, but so that as those who praise God we should pass beyond it, so that placed above it we may judge it, not joined to it and judged in it. Let us hasten to that good which does not move through places or roll along in time, and from which all natures in place and time receive their form and shape. To see it, let us purify the heart through faith in our Lord Jesus Christ, who says: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God” (Matthew 5:8). For it is not those eyes that must be prepared to see that good—the eyes by which this light is seen, spread through places and not whole everywhere, but having one part here and another elsewhere. Rather, let us purify that sight and sharpness of vision by which we see, as far as is allowed in this life, what is just and what is holy, and what the beauty of wisdom is. Whoever sees this places it far above the fullness of all spatial expanses, and he feels that to see it the sharpness of his mind is not spread through the expanses of places, but is steadied by an incorporeal power.
orientation: Augustine is concluding his argument that all natures are good insofar as they exist, and now turns the reader from loving lower temporal beauty to seeking the eternal good through faith in Christ.

title: Against the fantasies that deform God
english: Since fantasies are great enemies of that sight—fantasies which our thought, drawn from carnal sense, turns over and holds in the imagination—let us detest this heresy. It followed the credence of its own fantasies, and it scattered and spread the divine substance through the expanses of places, however infinite, as if it were a shapeless mass, and cut it off on one side so that it could find a place for evil. which it could not see was not a nature, but against nature. And it adorned that very evil with such form and forms and peace of parts thriving in each nature—because without these goods it could not think of any nature—so that the evils it finds fault with there are buried under a wealth of countless goods. But let this be the end of this book; in the remaining ones, with God permitting and helping, the rest of its ravings will be refuted.
orientation: Augustine is closing the treatise by urging rejection of Mani's heresy because its fantasies about God as a bodily mass led it to invent a place for evil.
